title: Numerical experience with a reduced Hessian method for large scale constrained optimization
contribution: Turns the Biegler-Nocedal-Schmid reduced-Hessian SQP into a practical code (Algorithm RHC) whose cross-term correction (Broyden or finite-difference) stabilizes coordinate-basis steps; an analytic example and a three-arm ablation on test, Hock-Schittkowski and CUTE problems show that the correction helps with poor bases at no large cost (pp. 2, 5-9, 13-19).
problem_entry: Dropping the cross term Z'WYp_Y works with orthonormal bases but gives poor directions with the affordable coordinate bases (p. 4); entered from the first author's inefficient runs on chemical process control problems (p. 19).
key_idea: Approximate the cross term by w_k, via a Broyden matrix S_k (no extra gradient) or finite differences (one extra gradient) used only near the solution; rescaled FD formula (2.7), damping zeta_k, bound (2.29); MA28 basis choice with a tenfold-growth test; quasi-Newton matrices mapped across basis changes; watchdog switched on late (pp. 5-13).
assumptions: Equality constraints only, to isolate the correction (p. 5); A_k full column rank (p. 3); nonsingular basis C and positive definite reduced Hessian (p. 4); convergence taken from [2], with redefinition (2.7) said to affect only Lemma 5.5 there (pp. 2, 6).
proof_devices: analytic example with adjustable theta: orthogonal bases give quadratic contraction, the coordinate basis without correction a theta-dependent poor step, the corrected step equals the orthogonal one (pp. 13-14; derivation pp. 19-21)
B_k = Z_k'Z_k replaces BFGS to keep the example analytic (p. 12)
permutation identity PZ = Z~R to transform B and S after a basis change (pp. 11-12)
experiments: DEC-ALPHA; arms No Correction / Broyden / RHC; FD and watchdog on when the KKT measure < 0.1; Example 3 poor basis n=80: 27(39/27), 19(28/19), 17(21/18), good basis 6(6/6) for all; Hock-Schittkowski without times; CUTE EIGENC2, EIGENCCO, ORTHREGA/C/D with CPU; Broyden-only uses the fewest gradient evaluations (pp. 15-18).
positioning: Builds on the authors' SIAM J. Optim. 1995 theory paper [2] and contrasts with reduced-Hessian methods that omit the cross term (refs [8, 13, 14, 19, 24, 30], among them Coleman-Conn, Gabay, Gilbert and Xie) (pp. 4, 11, 22).
writing: Novelty sentence in the abstract; scope of the repair stated plainly: it cannot help with adequate bases, only prevent poor performance (p. 14).
limits_future: Equality constraints only (p. 5); MA28 may return the same basis and forcing a new one is not yet coded (p. 11); Broyden-only may be preferable when gradients are expensive (p. 19); Table 1 defaults unreadable in this file (p. 9).

method_links.note: engine kept; only the cross-term component repaired, with an explicit KKT-error trigger for the FD version, safeguards (2.27)/(2.29), and an ablation
analytic example separates bases and corrected/uncorrected steps; runs read against [2]'s prediction that the correction helps only off-tangential paths
own-code ablation rather than rival codes, but prints where the full method loses (Broyden-only needs fewer gradients)

transferable: Build a two-variable analytic example whose parameter makes an omitted term's harm arbitrarily large, then show the repair restores the ideal behaviour (pp. 13-14, 19-21).
Ablate a repair with three arms (none, cheap approximation, full) and report gradient evaluations separately from function evaluations (pp. 16-18).

After a change of coordinates, transform the quasi-Newton matrix with a permutation identity instead of resetting it (pp. 11-12).

quotes.text: The correction term cannot be expected to improve the performance of the algorithm when the basis matrices are adequate, but should prevent poor performance from taking place.
This research was motivated by numerical tests on chemical process control problems performed, a few years ago, by the first author.

title: Algorithm 809: PREQN: Fortran 77 subroutines for preconditioning the conjugate gradient method
contribution: Fortran 77 package that builds limited-memory BFGS preconditioners from the CG directions of one linear solve to precondition the next system in a slowly varying SPD sequence, through a single call per CG iteration, with two pair-selection options and numeric advice on m (pp. 1-8).
problem_entry: Sequences of slowly varying SPD systems whose matrices are known only through products or are dense, as in Newton methods for optimization, PDEs and statistics (abstract, p. 2).
key_idea: BFGS equals CG on quadratics, so CG pairs (p_j, A p_j) define an L-BFGS approximation of A^-1 that preconditions the next system; uniform-sample (IOP=1, last pair always added) or last-m (IOP=2) selection; one call applies the preconditioner and passes the newest pair; BUILD flag for reuse (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: A_i symmetric positive definite (so s'y > 0) and slowly varying (pp. 2-3); no convergence theory.
experiments: Three finite-element matrices from [5], 51 right-hand sides each, preconditioner built on the first solve and reused for 50; average CG iterations for several m and both IOP; uniform sampling much better here but usually comparable; table values unreadable (pp. 7-8).
positioning: Implements the preconditioner of the companion SIAM J. Optim. paper [5]; contrasts cost with incomplete Cholesky (pp. 4, 10).
writing: Advice given as numbers (m in [4, 20]) and as an explicit flop break-even (pp. 4, 7, 8).
limits_future: Not always beneficial; pays only if a matvec costs more than about 24n operations (m=16, IOP=1), so unlikely for very sparse problems; BUILD=.FALSE. to be used with caution; users should experiment with m (pp. 7-8).

method_links.note: two selection rules that both performed well exposed as option IOP, plus a BUILD switch
own preconditioner scoped by structure: advocated only for unknown, dense or costly matrices; break-even says when it will not pay

quotes.text: Values of m, in the range [4, 20], are recommended for most problems, independently of the value of n.
Therefore the preconditioner is unlikely to be useful for very sparse problems.

title: Feasibility control in nonlinear optimization
contribution: Survey with analysis that names 'feasibility control' (progress toward feasibility at least comparable to a Cauchy step) and classifies Newton, SQP and interior methods by it against Powell's and Wächter-Biegler's counterexamples, adding an inefficiency example for NITRO's own inexact normal step (pp. 1-23).
problem_entry: Methods that demand exact satisfaction of constraint linearizations can converge to spurious non-stationary points; entered through Powell's nonlinear-equations example and the Wächter-Biegler interior example (abstract, pp. 2-4, 13-15).
key_idea: One property, feasibility control, sorts methods: LM, dogleg, Byrd-Omojokun, Celis-Dennis-Tapia and NITRO have it; Vardi, line-search Newton and interior methods and NUOPT lack it; SNOPT elastic mode supplies it only when needed; regularization is kept apart (pp. 4-22).
assumptions: Smooth functions; the TR result needs A(x) Lipschitz and bounded on the level set (p. 5); Byrd-Omojokun assumptions in a footnote (p. 9).
proof_devices: Powell's example: exact-line-search Newton converges to about (1.8016, 0.000), not stationary for the merit function (pp. 3-4)
Wächter-Biegler argument uses only the third Newton block plus bounds, so merit function and barrier update are irrelevant (p. 14)
singular KKT matrix on the limit manifold compared with Example 1, left open (p. 15)
Example 3 recurrence: range-space normal step cut by fraction-to-boundary gives an iteration lower bound (4.23) under Delta0 > (9/4)mu, s0 = mu (pp. 19-21)
experiments: Demonstration runs only: relaxed line search converges on Powell's example (p. 4); NITRO escapes Example 2 (Figure 3, p. 18); NITRO line-search option solves Example 3 in five steps, infeasibility 5.000E+02 to 6.706E-14 (Table 1, p. 21); slow feasibility also on CUTE GOFFIN (p. 21).
positioning: Credits Powell's analysis as a founding block of TR theory (p. 6), Wächter-Biegler for the interior counterexample (p. 13), NUOPT's excellent results while showing it fails Example 2 (pp. 21-22).
writing: Hedges placed where knowledge stops: 'We speculate' (p. 8), 'We do not know whether failures of this type are rare in practice' (p. 15), 'To our surprise' (p. 4).
limits_future: Open: a simple fix for line-search interior methods and whether Forsgren-Gill converges better (p. 15); new inexact subproblem techniques for Example 3 (p. 21); feasibility control in interior methods only beginning to be studied (p. 23).

method_links.note: external counterexample analysed as a specification; own solver's failure mode (NITRO inexact normal step on Example 3, GOFFIN) written down with a call for new techniques
Cauchy-decrease criterion separates methods that cannot fail on the examples from those that can
records where the own TR method loses, using the line-search option inside NITRO (like-with-like)

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: name one property (feasibility control) and classify about ten methods by it against canonical counterexamples

transferable: Organize a survey around one named mechanism and a few canonical counterexamples, and classify each method by whether it has the mechanism (pp. 2-22).
Before generalizing a counterexample proved for one line search, rerun it with a relaxed line search and from other starts (p. 4).
Turn a suspected inefficiency into a closed-form recurrence on a one-variable barrier problem that bounds the iteration count, then confirm with the alternative option in the same code (pp. 19-21).
coauthors: M. Marazzi (Northwestern IEMS) (p. 1); Byrd, Wächter, Waltz and Powell thanked (p. 23)

quotes.text: We should stress that failures of the line search Newton iteration (2.2) are observed in practical applications, and are not purely of academic interest.
We should stress that the interior method will not fail on Example 3, but that it will be inefficient.

title: Enriched methods for large-scale unconstrained optimization
contribution: Enriched method that interlaces L-BFGS and preconditioned Hessian-free Newton cycles with dynamically adjusted lengths and one shared limited-memory matrix; on large CUTE problems it uses 34371 function/gradient evaluations in total against 76224 and 75089 for two HFN variants (pp. 1-11).
problem_entry: HFN methods are notoriously sensitive to the inner CG termination rule; goal of parameter-free algorithms; HFN and L-BFGS strengths are complementary (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: l L-BFGS steps alternate with t HFN steps; H(m) both preconditions PCG and warm-starts L-BFGS; t=0 and l=0 give the parent methods; ADJUST sets l, t from step quality (profitable if alpha in [0.8, 1]), negative curvature and a force2 rule (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Gradients available, no second derivatives; Hessian-vector products by finite differences or AD; CG stops at negative curvature (pp. 2, 4); no convergence theory.
experiments: All large unconstrained CUTE problems; m=20, l=15; CG stop 30 iterations (5 at first) or residual ratio 1/10; HFN1 (Nash) and HFN2 (Dembo-Steihaug rule) with the same quasi-Newton preconditioner; totals 34371 / 76224 / 75089 evaluations; per-problem Enriched column lost in the text layer; no L-BFGS column (pp. 7-11).
positioning: Replaces the rigid Byrd-Nocedal-Zhu attempt (20 L-BFGS + 1 HFN, 5 unpreconditioned CG iterations) with a 'sophisticated implementation' (pp. 3-4).
writing: Claims of parameter insensitivity are asserted in the abstract and text without a table (abstract, pp. 4, 10); prose and ADJUST pseudocode disagree on two update rules (pp. 5-7).
limits_future: No limitations or future work printed; robustness claims rest on untabulated runs (pp. 4, 10).

method_links.note: integrates complementary algorithms (HFN and L-BFGS) in one dynamic family rather than crowning one
competitors given the authors' own preconditioner and the same stopping test; other HFN variants tried
plain L-BFGS, one end of the family and the obvious simple baseline, has no column; insensitivity claims untabulated

Another way of motivating our approach is to note that the strengths and weaknesses of the HFN and L-BFGS methods are complementary.

title: iNEOS: An interactive environment for nonlinear optimization
contribution: CORBA-based client-server environment in which the user keeps a confidential, expensive simulation and a remote L-BFGS-B server returns iterates from function and gradient values alone, demonstrated on a 10-parameter piezoelectric identification problem (pp. 1-12).
problem_entry: NEOS requires the whole model as AMPL/Fortran/C files, excluding proprietary, slow or multi-language models (p. 2).
key_idea: Quasi-Newton iterations need only x_k, f_k, g_k, which do not reveal the model; reverse communication over the Internet via CORBA with a solver Factory and an Init/NextIterate interface; Nexus and DCOM rejected with reasons (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Bound constraints only (general constraints would need second derivatives sent to the server); 2n+1 floats per exchange, negligible against minutes-to-hours simulations; up to 1 million variables envisioned (pp. 4-5).
experiments: Piezoelectric crystal model, 10 bounded parameters, finite-difference derivatives; synthetic target, start perturbed by 7.5%, 1% recovery target, about 10 minutes per f/g evaluation, client in California and server in Illinois; reported as successfully completed, details deferred to [3] (pp. 8-11).
positioning: Motivated by the success of the NEOS server; builds on the internal client-server design of TRON and L-BFGS(-B) (pp. 2-3).
writing: Short systems note; design trade-offs recorded with concrete reasons (pp. 4-5).
limits_future: No user-level security (anyone can view submitted data); solver-specific API, XML common interface proposed with overhead to be measured; general constraints future work (pp. 4, 12).

method_links.note: the f-and-g-only property that makes L-BFGS the general method (step 3) reused as a deployment property that hides the model

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: algorithm information structure as a deployment interface
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: reverse communication turned into a remote, model-hiding optimization service (compare S098 single-call interface)

transferable: List what the algorithm needs per iteration (2n+1 numbers) and size communication against evaluation time before choosing middleware (p. 5).

coauthors: Marcel Good, Jean-Pierre Goux (Northwestern), Victor Pereyra (Weidlinger Associates) (p. 1); Todd Plantenga thanked (p. 12)

quotes.text: In nonlinear optimization, an improved solution can be generated just by knowing the current iterate and the numerical values of the function and gradient at the current point.
Anyone has access to iNEOS and can view the data submitted to it.

title: Feasible interior methods using slacks for nonlinear optimization
contribution: Shows how slack resets turn infeasible slack-based interior methods into feasible ones, proves the reset is harmless when steps satisfy the linearized inequalities, repairs KNITRO's trust-region step by a modified Cauchy direction, and gives the first feasible-versus-infeasible comparison (216 CUTE problems, 181 vs 179 solved) (pp. 1-19).
problem_entry: Some applications need inequality-feasible iterates (objective undefined outside, early termination), most NLP interior codes are infeasible, and no study had compared the two (pp. 2, 17).
key_idea: Reset s <- g(x_T) before evaluating the merit function, so feasible and infeasible modes differ in two boxed instructions with the same linear systems; with equalities, impose r_g = 0 (Feasible Step Conditions) and recompute only the Cauchy direction of KNITRO's normal step from system (5.30) (pp. 4-5, 12-14).
assumptions: Smooth f, h, g; merit with chi infinite for s <= 0; step-merit compatibility; Theorem 4.1 needs Lipschitz chi and Jacobian and a step satisfying (4.15); Corollary 5.1 needs nu large enough (called not restrictive) and a point not stationary for ||h||^2 (pp. 3-4, 10, 14-15).
proof_devices: Theorem 4.1: reset perturbation O(||d_x||^2) against first-order decrease gamma||d||, so small steps are accepted (pp. 10-11)
backtracking cannot cure a violation of (4.15) since every scalar multiple keeps it (p. 12)
Corollary 5.1 transfers the result to the modified dogleg normal step (pp. 14-15)
equivalence with the classical Fiacco-McCormick barrier for exact primal-dual Newton steps (pp. 6-7)
experiments: GAUSSELM (385 equalities, 750 inequalities) fails before the repair as ||delta_s|| tracks Delta down to 1.2e-14, then is solved in 102 iterations (Tables 1-2, pp. 9, 16); 153 problems with equalities: differ on 45, failures 3 vs 17 (p. 16); feasible vs infeasible KNITRO on 216 CUTE problems: 181 vs 179 solved, 58 never entered feasible mode, log2 ratio plot on 119 (pp. 17-18); limits 1000 iterations and 60 CPU minutes (p. 25).
positioning: Frames trust-region step computations of Vardi, Celis-Dennis-Tapia, Powell-Yuan, Byrd-Omojokun and Yamashita-Yabe in one subproblem form (p. 11); relates slack resets to Fiacco-McCormick barriers (pp. 6-7).
writing: Null result reported as a surprise and read as good news for the option; a confound (shared slack adjustment) disclosed in the same section (pp. 17-19).
limits_future: The reject-infeasible-trials alternative can fail and its step modification was not explored, though called plausible (pp. 16-17); shared slack adjustment narrows the comparison (p. 19); keep inequality/slack identity in the formulation and reset before the merit evaluation (pp. 19-20).

method_links.note: engine kept; only the slack reset and, in KNITRO, only the Cauchy direction of the normal step change

plausible expectations about infeasible freedom put on trial for the first time; verdict scoped by untouched problems and unattributed wins

However, we use it in our comparison taking the view that all methods should be tested using their best implementation within the KNITRO framework.
